response:
Confirmed the drift, and read the three files to ground the proposal. I did **not** edit anything — these are eval fixtures whose drift is intentional, and the ask was to propose.

## What the scan actually says

Two findings, `crime_00011` (`action_label_drift`) and `crime_00012` (`copy_ia_drift`), with **byte-identical evidence**:

```
group: delete
aliases: archive, delete, remove
"archive" in 2 file(s): SeatList.tsx, TeamList.tsx
"delete"  in 2 file(s): TeamList.tsx, UserList.tsx
"remove"  in 2 file(s): SeatList.tsx, UserList.tsx
```

Both are `low` / confidence 0.6 / agent_risk 0.38 — the two lowest-ranked findings in a 12-finding report. This is cheap-to-fix hygiene, not an emergency.

The source confirms it, and adds a detail the JSON hides — the drift is **per-destination**, not just per-file:

| href | labels pointing at it | files |
|---|---|---|
| `/users/manage` | "Delete user", "Remove member" | UserList:7,8 |
| `/teams/manage` | "Archive team" | TeamList:6 |
| `/seats/manage` | "Delete the seat", "Remove member", "Archive member" | TeamList:7, SeatList:6,7 |

Every destination is labelled with more than one verb, and `/seats/manage` gets **three verbs from two different components**. That's the real defect: an agent asked to "wire up the delete flow" has no way to tell whether these are one action or three.

## Proposed canonical set

Split on *what survives the action*, not on tone:

| Verb | Means | Reversible | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Remove** | revoke an association; the person/record still exists elsewhere | n/a | member ↔ team/seat membership |
| **Delete** | destroy the record itself | no | the team, the user account |
| **Archive** | hide/retire, restorable | yes | **ban it here** — nothing in this fixture has an undo |

Object noun: **member** for a person-in-a-container, **team** for the container. Drop "user" and "seat" from labels.

## Changes, tied to findings

Both findings share one root cause, so one edit set clears both. Ordered by what I'd do first:

**1. `src/components/SeatList.tsx` — first.** Lines 6–7 give the same href two verbs on adjacent lines (`Remove member` / `Archive member`), and this is the destination TeamList also reaches into. It has to be settled before TeamList's stray can be pointed anywhere sensible.
→ collapse to a single `<NavItem label="Remove member" href="/seats/manage" />`. Kills the `archive` hit in this file (`crime_00011`/`00012` evidence line 3).

**2. `src/components/TeamList.tsx`.** Line 6 `"Archive team"` → `"Delete team"` (no undo exists, so `archive` is a lie). Line 7 `"Delete the seat"` doesn't belong here at all — it points at `/seats/manage`, another component's destination; delete the item and let SeatList own it. Clears the file's `archive` **and** `delete` hits.

**3. `src/components/UserList.tsx`.** Lines 7–8 are two labels for one href. If they're genuinely one action, collapse to `"Remove member"`; if the account-destruction action is real, it needs its own destination and the label `"Delete user"`. Either way, don't ship both verbs against `/users/manage`.

**One caveat worth stating plainly:** the detector needs ≥3 aliases each appearing in ≥2 files. Right now each alias sits at exactly 2 files, so **fixing any single component silences both findings** while the other two stay inconsistent. Don't treat the finding going green as proof the drift is gone — do all three.

Also below threshold and therefore invisible in this report: the *noun* drift. `user`/`member`/`seat` is a seeded group too, but "user" appears in 1 file and "seat" in 1 file, so only one alias qualifies and the group never fires. My proposal converges on "member", which is safe — it doesn't push any noun over the threshold.

## How the two detectors differ

They share the same analysis function (`packages/core/src/detectors/action-label-drift.ts:71`, `analyse(...)`). The only difference is the input filter:

- `action_label_drift` reads **JSX labels + nav entries + string-valued props** — the whole IA surface.
- `copy_ia_drift` passes `restrictToJsxLabel: true`, keeping only signals whose kind starts with `jsx_` (`action-label-drift.ts:91`), and skipping nav entries entirely (`:99`).

On *this* fixture the two sets are identical. `<NavItem label="…" />` matches `UI_LABEL_TAGS`, so the extractor tags every one of these five strings as `jsx_label` (`packages/language-js/src/parse/ui-strings.ts:30-41`) — which passes the JSX restriction. Same inputs → same fingerprint → duplicate finding. The only thing that differs in the output is `fix_shape` ("pick one verb per action" vs "pick the canonical label; redirect copies to it").

They'd diverge on a fixture where the drift lives outside JSX text — e.g. a `nav.ts` array with `{ label: "Archive team" }`, or a non-JSX label constant. `action_label_drift` fires; `copy_ia_drift` stays silent. That's the intended split: one detector covers the code surface, the other covers pure UI copy.

Two notes on reading the report:
- The `file` field on both findings (`SeatList.tsx`) is a **dedup anchor**, not a severity ranking — it's `allFiles[0]` after a lexicographic sort (`action-label-drift.ts:126-127`). SeatList happens to also be the right place to start, but the JSON isn't telling you that.
- Emitting both findings for one problem is arguably double-counting in the aggregate: the same drift contributes twice to the low-severity count. Worth considering suppressing `copy_ia_drift` when `action_label_drift` fired on the identical alias set and file list.
